fields.title: Smena: business owners leave in month two
fields.summary: Churn is rising, support is flooded with messages, but metrics look normal. Decide where to start investigating.
fields.decisionPrompt: Where will the team start next week?
fields.brief/role: You are the sole product manager at Smena.
fields.brief/company: Smena is a shift scheduling service for small cafes and stores. The owner pays, while the owner and employees use it. 1,400 paying accounts.
fields.brief/context: For three consecutive months, month two subscription churn has been rising: from 9% to 16%. The founder wants a plan for Monday. Support received 62 messages over the month that no one analyzed systematically. The analyst sent a product summary, and a marketing colleague drafted an interview script, offering to call eight churned owners this week.
fields.brief/objective: Understand what actually causes churn before the team spends a sprint.
fields.brief/constraints: You and two developers. One week until Monday. Data is available for only the last month; a longer extract will take the analyst two days.
fields.brief/task: Decide where the team will start and explain what your decision is based on.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: First analyze what you already have
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Before collecting new data, see what can be extracted from what's already collected. Categorizing feedback by task and breaking down averages into distributions takes hours and often reframes the question entirely. New research started before doing this asks questions whose answers will have to be thrown away anyway.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
62 support messages. Raw list, sorted by date.

By word frequency: "inconvenient" — 17 times, "confusing" — 15, "doesn't work" — 11.

The four longest and most detailed emails came from a single account — a chain of six locations. All four were about accounting reports. The chain owner writes at length and persistently; support remembers him.

The rest of the messages are short, one or two lines, mostly coming from employee email addresses rather than owners.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Over the last 30 days:
- DAU 3,900, up 6% month-over-month
- Average shift swaps per account: 3.1
- Average owner logins per week: 2.4
- Share of accounts saving a schedule for the next week: 71%

Analyst note: "I used a 30-day window because deeper data isn't ready. All numbers are averages across all paying accounts; I didn't break them down by segment. Tell me what you need."

A shift swap histogram is attached separately but not described in the email.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Eight calls with owners who didn't renew. Draft questions:

1. Was Smena convenient to use?
2. How often do you usually build schedules?
3. Would employee shift notifications be helpful?
4. What was missing from the product?
5. Would you return if we built accounting reports?

Colleague comment: "List approved, can start calling tomorrow. If we need changes, let's do it today — slots are already booked."
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Subscription: 1,900 ₽/month per location. Average account has 1.4 locations.

Month two churn: 9% → 16% over three months. Churn after month six is consistently under 3% — those who survive stay long-term.

Accounting reports requested by the six-location chain are estimated by developers at two weeks.

Founder: "I don't need pretty analysis. I need to know what we're building this sprint."
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Categorize feedback and segment metrics, then call owners
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Spend one to two days: categorize 62 messages by what the person was doing; segment metrics by owners vs employees and inspect distributions instead of averages. Rewrite script based on what analysis reveals.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Categorization takes a day and a half. The picture changes: out of 62 messages, 41 come from employee emails, mostly in "shift swap / unclear if confirmed." Four accounting emails came from a single account — a single voice.
The histogram shows 64% of accounts never made a swap, while the remaining 36% had a median of 8 per month. The 3.1 average described nobody.
Calls are postponed by two days with a rewritten script: instead of "was it convenient," ask "show how you built schedules in the final week before you stopped." Six out of eight owners show they went back to spreadsheets because employees kept asking them in messaging apps anyway.
By Monday, the founder has a mechanism rather than a list of topics.
Trade-off: you spent two days of the week and shifted calls booked by your colleague.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The most detailed and persistent requests are for reports. Spend two weeks of dev time to address the most talked-about issue.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Reports launch in two and a half weeks. The six-location chain is happy and stays.
Month two churn remains unchanged: 16% next month and 15% the month after. Post-mortem reveals the four emails were from one account, while 41 of 62 messages came from employees regarding shift swaps.
The founder asks why two weeks went to a customer who wasn't leaving anyway.
Trade-off: you fixed the most visible issue and spent a sprint without verifying if it was connected to churn at all.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Call eight owners using the ready script
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Slots are booked, and churned owners are the most direct source. Conduct eight calls this week and bring insights on Monday.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Eight calls happen over three days. Six owners reply "overall it was convenient," seven say notifications "would be helpful," five say they would return for reports.
On Monday, the team brings the conclusion: notifications and reports are needed. One and a half months after releasing notifications, month two churn is 15%.
In the next review, someone notes question 3 led the answer, question 5 offered a solution, and no question asked what people actually did.
Trade-off: you got quick answers to questions that measured politeness rather than behavior.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: "Confusing" is the second most common phrasing, and shift swaps are mentioned most often. Resolve support's top topic with notifications.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Notifications launch in a week. "Unclear if swap confirmed" messages drop threefold; employees are happy.
Owner churn in month two falls from 16% to 13% — noticeable, but below expectations. Later it turns out 64% of accounts don't use swaps at all, so nothing changed for them; the gain came solely from the active third.
Trade-off: you guessed a real issue and applied it to everyone without checking that it applied to only a third of accounts.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Feedback was not categorized by what the user was trying to do
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Volume of noise was mistaken for problem severity
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: An average was taken as a description of user behavior
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A metric was named without a goal or an observable signal
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Interview questions ask about the future or about "usually"
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Research was planned without a falsifiable hypothesis
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: A customer's feature request was mistaken for their underlying problem
